title: Self Induction
short_intro: Self induction is the phenomenon by which a changing current in a single electric circuit induces an opposing electromotive force (emf) within the same circuit. The magnitude of this induced emf is proportional to the time rate of change of the current through the inductor.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of self-inductance, factors affecting self-inductance, self-inductance of a long solenoid, and growth/decay of current in an L-R circuit.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Detailed field-theoretic derivation of magnetic energy density stored in an inductor, coefficient of self-induction for complex geometries like toroidal coils, and transient response analysis in coupled inductive circuits.

prerequisites: Lenz's law and magnetic flux definition
Ampere's circuital law and magnetic field of a solenoid

concept_notes.heading: Origin and Nature of Self-Induction
bullets: When a varying electric current passes through a coil, the magnetic flux linked with each turn of the coil changes in proportion to the current.
By Faraday's law, this change in flux induces an emf in the coil itself, termed as the back emf.
According to Lenz's law, this induced emf always opposes the change in current that produces it, acting as electrical inertia.

concept_notes.heading: Coefficient of Self-Induction (Self-Inductance)
bullets: Magnetic flux linkage NΦ is directly proportional to the current I flowing through the circuit, given by NΦ = L I.
The constant of proportionality L is defined as the coefficient of self-induction or self-inductance of the coil.
Self-inductance depends strictly on the geometrical parameters of the conductor, number of turns, and the magnetic permeability of the core medium.

concept_notes.heading: Stored Magnetic Energy in an Inductor
bullets: Work must be done by an external source to establish a current against the opposing self-induced back emf.
This electrical work is stored entirely within the magnetic field enclosed by the inductor.
The total magnetic potential energy stored when current reaches steady value I is given by U = (1/2) L I².

concept_notes.heading: Growth and Decay of Current in L-R Circuit
bullets: When a DC voltage source is connected to a series combination of resistor R and inductor L, the current grows exponentially according to I = (V/R)(1 - exp(-t/τ)).
The time constant τ = L/R characterizes the rate at which the current approaches its maximum steady-state value.
During decay, when the voltage source is shorted, the current decays exponentially as I = I_0 exp(-t/τ).

derivations.title: Self-Inductance of a Long Solenoid
derivations.conditions: Air-core long solenoid of length l, cross-sectional area A, and total turns N, where l is much greater than its radius.
steps: Write the magnetic field inside an ideal long solenoid carrying current I: B = mu_0 n I, where n = N/l is the number of turns per unit length.
Calculate the magnetic flux Φ through a single turn of the solenoid: Phi = B A = mu_0 left( rac{N}{l}ight) I A.
Determine the total magnetic flux linkage for N turns: NPhi = N left[ mu_0 left( rac{N}{l}ight) I A ight] =  rac{mu_0 N^2 A}{l} I.
Equate total flux linkage to L I to extract the self-inductance L: L =  rac{NPhi}{I} =  rac{mu_0 N^2 A}{l}.
derivations.result: L =  rac{mu_0 N^2 A}{l} or in terms of magnetic permeability mu and small n: L = mu n^2 A l

derivations.title: Energy Stored in an Inductor
derivations.conditions: An inductor of self-inductance L carrying a growing current I at any instant t.
steps: The instantaneous power supplied to overcome the back emf e is P = e I, where magnitude of back emf is e = L  rac{dI}{dt}.
Express the incremental work done dW in time dt as dW = P dt = left( L  rac{dI}{dt} ight) I dt = L I dI.
Integrate the incremental work from initial current 0 to final steady current I_0: U = int_{0}^{I_0} L I dI.
Evaluate the integral to obtain the total magnetic energy: U = L left[  rac{I^2}{2} ight]_{0}^{I_0} =  rac{1}{2} L I_0^2.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Growth of Current in an L-R Circuit
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of current I on the y-axis versus time t on the x-axis, showing an asymptotic exponential curve approaching maximum value I_0 = V/R, with a tangent at t=0 intersecting the asymptote at t = 	au.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Indicates the inertia of the inductor delaying the instantaneous rise of current due to back emf.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Questions testing the definition of time constant as the time required for current to reach (1 - 1/e) or about 63.2% of its maximum value.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Decay of Current in an L-R Circuit
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A downward sloping exponential decay curve of current I versus time t starting from initial value I_0 and asymptotically approaching zero.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Represents the dissipation of stored magnetic energy through the resistor when the driving voltage source is removed.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Evaluating current magnitude at t = 	au, where current falls to 1/e (approx 36.8%) of its initial value.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Magnetic Flux Linkage versus Current
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line passing through the origin on a NPhi vs I coordinate system.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of this linear graph represents the constant coefficient of self-induction L for linear ferromagnetic or air-core systems.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical interpretation where slope calculation yields self-inductance.

solved_numericals.question: A coil of 500 turns has a magnetic flux of 4 	imes 10^{-3} Wb linked with it when a current of 2 A flows through it. Calculate the self-inductance of the coil.
solution_steps: Identify given values: N = 500, Phi = 4 	imes 10^{-3} Wb, I = 2 A.
Use the formula for flux linkage: NPhi = L I.
Substitute the values: 500 	imes 4 	imes 10^{-3} = L 	imes 2.
Calculate L: 2 = 2 L implies L = 1 H.

solved_numericals.question: A long solenoid has 1000 turns per meter and a cross-sectional area of 10 cm^2. If a current of 5 A flows through it, calculate the total magnetic energy stored in the solenoid within a length of 0.5 meters.
solution_steps: Find self-inductance per unit length or total inductance for length l = 0.5 m. Using n = 1000 m^{-1}, N = n 	imes l = 1000 	imes 0.5 = 500 turns.
Convert area to SI units: A = 10 cm^2 = 10 	imes 10^{-4} m^2 = 10^{-3} m^2.
Calculate self-inductance L using formula L = mu_0 n^2 A l: L = (4pi 	imes 10^{-7}) 	imes (1000)^2 	imes (10^{-3}) 	imes 0.5.
Evaluate L: L = (4pi 	imes 10^{-7}) 	imes 10^6 	imes 10^{-3} 	imes 0.5 = (4pi 	imes 10^{-4}) 	imes 0.5 = 2pi 	imes 10^{-4} H.
Calculate stored magnetic energy U = (1/2) L I^2 with I = 5 A: U = 0.5 	imes (2pi 	imes 10^{-4}) 	imes (5)^2.
Evaluate U: U = pi 	imes 10^{-4} 	imes 25 = 25pi 	imes 10^{-4} J approx 7.85 	imes 10^{-3} J.

solved_numericals.question: An inductor of inductance 2 H and negligible resistance is connected across a source of emf. If the current changes at a constant rate of 10 A/s, find the magnitude of the induced back emf and the power absorbed by the inductor at t = 2 seconds.
solution_steps: Recall the formula for induced emf: e = L  rac{dI}{dt}.
Substitute given values: L = 2 H and  rac{dI}{dt} = 10 A/s.
Power absorbed by the inductor against back emf is given by P = e I. Since current increases at 10 A/s, at t = 2 s, current I = (dI/dt) 	imes t = 10 	imes 2 = 20 A.
Calculate power: P = 20 V 	imes 20 A = 400 W.

assumptions_and_limitations: The formulas assume a linear magnetic core where magnetic permeability mu remains constant and independent of the applied magnetic field strength (absence of magnetic saturation and hysteresis losses).

common_misconceptions.wrong: An inductor opposes the flow of electric current through it.
common_misconceptions.correct: An inductor opposes only the change in electric current, not the steady current itself.
common_misconceptions.why: When current is steady (dI/dt = 0), the induced emf is zero, and a pure inductor acts as a simple conducting wire with zero resistance.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Self-inductance depends on the magnitude of current flowing through the coil.
common_misconceptions.correct: Self-inductance is purely a geometric and material property of the inductor.
common_misconceptions.why: Although flux linkage NPhi is proportional to current I, their ratio L = NPhi/I remains constant for a rigid geometrical configuration.

quick_revision: Self-inductance L represents electrical inertia, measured in Henry (H) or Wb/A.
Stored magnetic energy in an inductor is given by U = (1/2) L I^2.
Time constant of an L-R circuit is 	au = L/R, representing the inertia of transient response.
